walkthroughs.body_html:
Forces & Motion — a core area of GCSE Physics.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Forces & Motion brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Forces & Motion.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: A 2 kg object accelerates at 4 m/s². What is the resultant force?
options: 2 N
8 N
6 N

mcqs.q: What does it mean if the resultant force on an object is zero?
options: The object must be stationary.
The object is either stationary or moving at constant velocity.
The object is decelerating.
The object is accelerating.

mcqs.q: If an object is moving at constant velocity in a straight line, what is the net force on it?
options: The wall pushes back with a force proportional to how stiff it is, not equal to your force.
The net force equals the velocity times the mass of the object.
Zero — by Newton's first law, constant velocity requires zero net force.
There must be a forward force on the object to keep it moving.

mcqs.q: When you push a wall, what does Newton's third law say about the wall?
options: The wall only pushes back if your force is strong enough to make it react.
The wall pushes back with a force proportional to how stiff it is, not equal to your force.
The wall exerts an equal and opposite force on you at the same instant.
The net force equals the velocity times the mass of the object.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between mass and weight?
options: The net force equals the velocity times the mass of the object.
Mass and weight are the same thing, just expressed in different units.
Mass is the amount of matter (kg); weight is the gravitational force on that mass (N) and depends on g.
Mass changes with location but weight does not.
